topic_title: Old Money Christmas Decor: 10 Classic Ideas That Look Inherited
intro: The old money look is less about spending and more about restraint. It borrows from country houses: deep green, burgundy, navy and brass, real or convincing greenery, and things that look as if they have been brought out every December for decades. Limit the palette to two colors plus brass, choose fewer pieces in better materials, and skip anything with words on it. Mixing in one or two genuinely old items, such as thrifted brass or a family ornament, does more for the look than another new set.

picks.description: A magnolia leaf garland is the single piece most associated with the old money Christmas look. The leaves are glossy dark green on top and velvety brown underneath, so a garland shows both colors and looks rich without any ornaments. Drape it along the mantel so it hangs a few inches over each end, or run it down a staircase banister with wire ties. A six-foot faux garland covers most mantels; for a fuller look, layer it over a plain pine or cedar garland. Fresh magnolia is available from florists and Southern tree lots but browns in two to three weeks indoors and can mark painted wood, so set it on a runner. Good faux versions cost more than average garlands but last many seasons, which fits the inherited idea.
picks.best_for: Mantels and staircases that need one big classic statement
picks.skip_if: You want a bright, colorful Christmas; magnolia reads deep and formal
picks.quirky_fact: Magnolia garlands became a Southern holiday tradition partly because the trees keep their leaves all winter.

picks.description: Brass candlesticks with tall taper candles are the quickest way to make a room look old money, because brass is the metal of country houses and antiques. Group three or five at different heights on a mantel, sideboard or dining table rather than lining up a matched pair. Mismatched brass is fine and even better, which makes thrift stores and estate sales good places to look, often for a few dollars each. Use ivory, deep green or burgundy tapers in 10 or 12 inch lengths. Real flame needs attention around greenery, so keep at least a few inches between candle and garland, or use LED tapers with a realistic wax finish. Clean tarnish with a brass polish, but a little patina helps the look.
picks.best_for: Tables, mantels and sideboards that need height and warm light
picks.skip_if: You have curious toddlers or cats near tabletops and won't use LED tapers
picks.quirky_fact: Unlacquered brass darkens over time, and many collectors leave that patina because it shows age.
picks.product_name: Brass Taper Candle Holders Set of 3

picks.description: Velvet bows in deep red, green or navy replace most of the ornaments in an old money scheme. Tie large bows with long tails and wire them onto the tree, garland, wreath, chair backs and the tops of stockings so the same bow repeats through the room. Repetition is what makes simple decor look planned. Buy velvet ribbon by the roll, 2.5 inches wide for the tree and 4 inches for wreaths and doors, and tie the bows yourself, which costs far less than pre-made ones. Wired-edge velvet holds its shape best. Real velvet crushes in storage, so pack bows loosely in a box with tissue. On a tree, about 15 to 20 large bows suit a seven-foot tree, spaced evenly from top to bottom.
picks.best_for: Pulling the tree, mantel and doors into one color scheme
picks.skip_if: You want a tree full of ornaments; bows work best with fewer other pieces
picks.quirky_fact: Velvet ribbon in a single color often looks more expensive than mixed patterned ribbon, because the eye reads it as one deliberate choice.
picks.product_name: Wired Velvet Ribbon 2.5 Inch x 10 Yards, Burgundy

picks.description: A boxwood wreath is the classic front door and window wreath of traditional homes. Its small, tight leaves give a neat, clipped look instead of the shaggy outline of pine. Hang one on the front door with a velvet bow, or hang smaller ones on each window with ribbon for a symmetrical facade that reads very old money from the street. Indoors, a boxwood wreath over a mirror or above a mantel works too. Fresh preserved boxwood lasts months indoors but fades in direct sun; faux boxwood holds up outdoors for several winters and is the easier choice for doors. Sizes from 16 to 22 inches suit most front doors. Keep the decoration to one bow so the shape stays clean.
picks.best_for: Front doors and windows that need a neat, traditional look
picks.skip_if: Your door gets strong afternoon sun, which fades preserved boxwood quickly
picks.quirky_fact: Boxwood has been used in formal gardens for centuries because it tolerates tight clipping into shapes.

picks.description: A tartan throw puts the whole old money palette into one piece: deep red, green, navy and a thin yellow or white stripe. Fold it over the arm of a sofa or the end of a bed, or lay it under a tree in place of a tree skirt. Wool or a wool blend looks right and keeps its shape; cheap fleece prints look thin and pill quickly. One tartan in a room is usually enough, with other textiles kept plain in one of its colors, such as a green velvet pillow. A good throw is not seasonal either, so it can stay out from November through February. Wool needs spot cleaning or dry cleaning rather than the washing machine, so keep drinks and pets with muddy paws in mind.
picks.best_for: Sofas and beds that need instant winter color and warmth
picks.skip_if: You need machine-washable textiles because of kids or pets
picks.quirky_fact: Many tartans are tied to particular Scottish clans or regions, though plenty sold today are newer designs.

picks.description: Velvet stockings with a stitched initial or name look like heirlooms and replace the novelty stockings that break the old money mood. Choose one color for everyone, such as deep green or burgundy velvet with a cream cuff, and let the monogram tell them apart. Matching stockings hung evenly across the mantel look far more classic than a mix of patterns. Many shops embroider initials for a small fee, or you can add iron-on or hand-stitched letters. Hang them from brass stocking holders on the mantel shelf, or from small hooks under a garland if you don't want weight on the shelf. The trade-off is cost per stocking, which adds up for big families, so start with the household and add more later.
picks.best_for: Families who want stockings that look the same every year
picks.skip_if: Your kids want character or themed stockings they picked themselves
picks.quirky_fact: Monograms in matching stockings usually use the first initial alone, which keeps the set looking uniform.
picks.product_name: Personalized Velvet Christmas Stocking with Embroidered Name

picks.description: Blue and white ginger jars are a staple of traditional American and English interiors, and at Christmas they become containers for greenery. Fill one with cut magnolia, pine or holly branches, or set a pair on either side of the mantel with garland running between them. The blue looks fresh beside deep green and brass and adds a second color without breaking the classic mood. Many people already own one, and thrift stores often carry them at low prices. Large jars with lids work as decor alone, while open vases hold stems; a plastic liner or jar inside protects the glaze from water. They stay out all year, which means you aren't buying something for one month.
picks.best_for: Rooms that already have blue tones or year-round chinoiserie
picks.skip_if: Your palette is red and gold, where the blue will fight for attention
picks.quirky_fact: Ginger jars were originally used to ship spices like ginger from China, which is how they got their name.
picks.product_name: Blue and White Porcelain Ginger Jar with Lid, Large

picks.description: Needlepoint pillows are a quiet signal of the old money style because they look handmade and slightly old-fashioned. Christmas designs usually show a nutcracker, a wreath, a dog in a bow, a tartan or a simple holly sprig. One or two on a sofa is enough; set them against plain velvet or linen pillows so the stitching stands out. A dog or nutcracker design brings a little humor without tipping into novelty. Ready-made needlepoint pillows range widely in price, with wool needlepoint costing more than printed lookalikes. If you like crafts, a needlepoint kit takes many evenings but becomes a real heirloom piece. Store them in a breathable bag in a dry closet between seasons, since wool attracts moths.
picks.best_for: Sofas and reading chairs that need a handmade, traditional detail
picks.skip_if: You prefer minimal decor and plain cushions
picks.quirky_fact: Needlepoint is stitched on a stiff open-weave canvas, which is why the pillows keep a firm, flat face.

picks.breed: Paperwhite Bulbs in a Silver Bowl
picks.description: Paperwhites are white, fragrant narcissus that bloom indoors without soil, and a bowl of them is a traditional winter centerpiece. Plant the bulbs close together in a silver or pewter bowl on a layer of pebbles, add water just to the base of the bulbs, and they bloom in about four to six weeks. Start in mid-November for flowers at Christmas. The plain white flowers and green stems fit the palette without adding another color. Stems can flop as they grow tall, so tie them loosely with ribbon or twine. The scent is strong, and some people find it unpleasant in small rooms, so try one bowl before planting several. Bulbs are toxic to pets and should stay out of reach.
picks.best_for: Dining tables and entry tables that need living flowers in winter
picks.skip_if: You have pets that chew plants or dislike strong floral scents
picks.quirky_fact: A small splash of alcohol in the water is a common gardener's trick to keep paperwhite stems shorter.

picks.description: A tray with a crystal decanter and a few glasses is the entertaining corner of the old money look. Set it on a sideboard, bar cart or library shelf, with a brass or silver tray underneath and a small sprig of greenery or a bow on the decanter's neck. Cut crystal catches candlelight in the evening, which is when the look matters most. A decanter works for whisky, port or simply water and juice for guests. Look for lead-free crystal if you plan to keep drinks in it for days. Thrift stores and estate sales often have decanters and stemware at a fraction of the price of new ones. Keep it out of reach of kids, as heavy crystal breaks if pulled off a low surface.
picks.best_for: Hosts who entertain in December and have a sideboard or cart
picks.skip_if: You don't serve drinks at home or have small children near low surfaces
picks.quirky_fact: Decanting was originally used to separate wine from sediment, not for looks.
picks.product_name: Lead-Free Crystal Whiskey Decanter Set with 4 Glasses

faqs.question: What colors are used in old money Christmas decor?
faqs.answer: Deep green, burgundy or oxblood red, navy and cream are the core colors, with brass or antique gold as the metal. Tartan brings several of these together in one fabric. Avoid bright red and green together, silver glitter and neon lights. Pick two main colors, repeat them on the tree, mantel and table, and let brass tie the rooms together.

faqs.question: How do I get the old money Christmas look on a budget?
faqs.answer: Spend on the few pieces people see first, such as a full garland on the mantel and a pair of brass candlesticks, and save elsewhere. Thrift stores and estate sales are good sources for brass, silver bowls and blue and white china, often for a few dollars each. Cut fresh greenery from your yard or buy clippings from a tree lot, and tie bows yourself from velvet ribbon by the roll.

faqs.question: Is fresh or faux greenery better for this style?
faqs.answer: Fresh greenery smells and looks the most authentic, but magnolia and boxwood dry out within a few weeks indoors, especially near a fireplace. A good approach is a realistic faux garland as the base with a few fresh stems tucked in for scent and texture. Faux pieces last for years, which suits the idea of decor that comes back every December.

faqs.question: Can I mix old money decor with a modern home?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as the pieces stay classic in shape and material. A tartan throw on a modern sofa, brass candlesticks on a plain console and a garland on a simple mantel all work. Keep the room mostly to two holiday colors and brass, and leave out novelty pieces, so the traditional items read as intentional rather than out of place.

faqs.question: When should old money Christmas decor go up?
faqs.answer: Many traditional households wait until early December, and some put the tree up only a week or two before Christmas. Faux garlands, wreaths, throws and brass can go up whenever you like. Plan fresh greenery and paperwhites for the middle of December so they look their best on the days you entertain.

seo_title: Old Money Christmas Decor 2026: 10 Classic Ideas
answer: A magnolia leaf garland, brass candlesticks with taper candles and velvet ribbon bows do most of the work in old money Christmas decor. The deciding factor is materials: real greenery, metal, wool and velvet read as inherited, while glitter, plastic and slogans do not.
method: Picked from Pinterest's trending searches for old money Christmas decor in late October 2026, then ordered by how much of the look each idea creates for its cost and effort, and how many seasons it lasts.
author: Elena Marsh
